scenarios.action: Designate him for assignment (or put him on outright waivers)
scenarios.text: The club has 7 days to trade him, pass him through outright waivers, or release him; he is paid at the major-league rate and keeps accruing service in the meantime. On outright waivers any club can claim him for $50,000, worst record first, and the claiming club takes his contract (1 yr, $3.55M (2026)). Three-plus years of service give him the Article XX-D choice: elect free agency immediately (giving up the rest of his salary) or accept the assignment, keep getting paid, and elect free agency after the season unless he is added back to a 40-man first. Post-season: an outright after the September 1 cutoff ends his automatic eligibility. He could only return as an approved injury replacement, and only if he accepts the outright and stays on a minor-league reserve list in the organization without interruption; a release makes him ineligible for anyone this October. With real money left on the contract a claim is unlikely; the usual outcome is clearing waivers, then release, with the club paying the balance less what a new club pays him.

Release waivers cost a claiming club $1 but the claimant assumes the whole contract, so expensive players clear. The club owes the full unpaid balance of this season's salary, offset by whatever another club pays him this year. A released player is not post-season eligible for any club this year.
Not now: players on major-league contracts cannot be traded after the Aug 3 deadline until the day after the World Series.

At the tender deadline (Nov 20) the club can decline to offer a contract: no waivers, no termination pay, and he can be re-signed the same night. Tendering means arbitration, where he cannot be cut more than 20% from this year's salary.
